newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel unions step up strikes ahead of budget vote.
newsitem.headline: Israel unions step up strikes ahead of budget vote.

text.p: More than a quarter of a million striking workers crippled large sectors of Israel's economy on Monday, stepping up protests against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's austerity plans ahead of a vote on the 1997 budget.
The Histadrut labour federation said 283,000 public sector employees staged walkouts on Monday as the largest of four days of strikes brought much of the economy to a halt.
Government and induatry officials put economic damage from the strikes at tens of millions of dollars.

Banks, government offices and the Tel Aviv stock exchange were closed. Public hospitals, ambulances and firefighters went on emergency schedules and phone, transportation and postal services were disrupted.
Seaports were closed for a fourth day running and state-owned radio and television broadcasts were scaled back. Airports, which were shut down on Sunday, remained open.
Monday's strike was to last until 4 p.m. (1400 GMT).

Netanyahu has blasted the strikes, the largest grassroots challenge to his budget-slashing plans, as "irresponsible" and "baseless". Finance Minister Dan Meridor threatened on Sunday to take unspecified action against the picketers.
Treasury sources said Meridor had no plans to meet Histadrut leaders on Monday. Industrialists also condemned the disruptions.

"We see this strike as political. We think political disputes should be settled in political ways and not on the backs of the business sector which is suffering severely," said Manufacturers' Association President Danny Gillerman.
"We estimate the damage from the strikes in the ports alone at around $10 million a day," he told Israel Radio.
Last Thursday the Histadrut launched a series of gradually widening walkouts that were due to culminate in a general strike on Tuesday, when parliament was set to vote the 1997 budget.

The government's 1997 proposal calls for seven billion shekels ($2.15 billion) in spending cuts, new taxes and other revenue-raising measures that Netanyahu said were needed to rein in soaring deficits.
Union leaders say the cuts will erode workers salaries.

"The workers alone will be forced to pay the price...for the government's big exercise in fraud. Next year the salary of every worker will be eroded by 2,500 to 3,000 shekels," said Histadrut chief Amir Peretz.
"These aren't battle games or arm-twisting games," he told Israel radio. "There is a need to reach agreements."

The Histadrut demands Netanyahu cancel proposals to delink income tax brackets to inflation and opposes elimination of a special tax credit for working women. Union leaders were blasted for shutting down the economy over such limited objectives.

"Nobody knows why the workers are striking," Finance Ministry Director General David Brodet told Army Radio. "The Histadrut in some respects was looking for an excuse to strike to show the government it still exists on the street."
Peretz partially concurred, saying the Histadrut wanted to ensure a place at the table when Netanyahu unveils a promised privatisation programme.
"They shouldn't be surprised (of future action) if later workers are not partners on much more important issues," he told Israel Radio.

Thousands of workers walked off their jobs on Sunday and others ignored court orders to show up for work after police arrested trade union leader Shlomo Shani for failing to appear before a labour court in connection with strike violations.
"Strikes are legitimate...but the law must be respected," Finance Minister Dan Meridor told Israel Radio.
($1=3.26 shekels)
